entry.content:
The Midterm Elections — The Last Entry of the Day

Objective

The Rally Is Gone and the Count Is Not Finished

The last entry of the day at 0000: Thursday’s closes are fixed and lower, the futures fall again in the evening, Tokyo opens its Friday in a slide that carries the Nikkei into a bear market, Brent trades back toward a hundred dollars on an expanded tanker file, and the count—two Senate seats, two governorships, and the last House races, Colorado’s among them—goes to Friday unfinished.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 0000 ET, Friday, November 6, 2026—the midnight that begins this date and closes the day before it. This edition completes the log of November 5 begun in Edition No. 6, the Overnight Watch, continued in Edition No. 7, the Midday Watch, and carried whole in Edition No. 8, the Evening Watch, with Special Report No. 1 filed outside the watches at 1912. Those editions stand unrevised, as a log stands. Where the midnight figures differ from the evening figures, the difference is stated here, in the open—and in Colorado’s 3rd District they differ in the leader, not only in the margin.

What Thursday Settled

Thursday’s closes are fixed, and they are the day’s largest settled fact. The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed down 1,833.06 points, or 3.44 percent, at 51,523.06, against a gain of 1,569.40 points on Wednesday. The S&P 500 closed down 4.36 percent at 7,353.73, its worst day since April 2025. The Nasdaq Composite closed down 5.52 percent at 24,315.00, in correction territory, 11.9 percent below its October 6 record close. The Nasdaq 100 closed down 6.36 percent at 26,629.81, the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 12.25 percent to 9,011.14, and the Russell 2000, in the evening futures account filed below, lost 4.5 percent. The volatility index closed at 28.09, up 69.1 percent, and the ten-year Treasury yield slipped about six basis points to roughly 4.84 percent. All three principal indexes closed below their levels of Tuesday, election day. The figures stand as the Evening Watch printed them, from the closing account; midnight adds nothing to them except the hours after them, which are filed below.

The day’s economic figures are also fixed, and they run the other way. Initial claims for unemployment benefits stand at 189,000 for the week ended October 31, down 6,000, the lowest reading since 1969, per Reuters’ report of the Labor Department’s releases; third-quarter productivity rose at a 3.6 percent annualized rate and unit labor costs fell 0.7 percent. In London, Bank Rate stands at 4 percent, raised from 3.75 percent by 8–1, per Reuters’ Bank of England file. Control of Congress and of the governorships stands settled as it stood on Wednesday: the Senate at 54 seats for the Democrats and 44 for the Republicans, the governorships at 28 for the Democrats, and the Democrats to organize the House in January. What Thursday added to the settled column was calls. The Associated Press called Colorado’s 5th District for the Democrat, Jessica Killin, in the afternoon. In the evening the wire called New York’s 17th District for the Democrat, Cait Conley, at 140,165 votes to the incumbent Republican Mike Lawler’s 128,292, per the district file—two days after Lawler called Conley himself to concede on election night, per the account of the networks’ confirmation filed below. The running live file recorded the evening’s other calls in sequence: Democrats flip Arizona’s 6th, Colorado’s 5th, Montana’s 1st, and North Carolina’s 9th Districts at 5:55 p.m. ET, and New York’s 17th at 6:44 p.m.

The Count at Midnight

No Senate race was called on Thursday, for the second full day, and the two open races end the day where the evening left them. The Associated Press Senate file in its latest state lists Alaska and Mississippi as too early to call, Mississippi at 99.83 percent of precincts reporting. The newest figures under the two races are Decision Desk HQ’s. In Mississippi, in the file’s update of 4:12 p.m. EST carried in the live results file filed below, the Democrat, Scott Colom, stands at 466,763 votes and the incumbent Republican, Cindy Hyde-Smith, at 464,939—a lead of 1,824 votes, at the top of the range this paper printed during the day, with more than 95 percent of the estimated vote counted. In Alaska the same file carries the Democrat, Mary Peltola, at 102,962 first-choice votes and the incumbent Republican, Dan Sullivan, at 102,325—a lead of 637. The dates that govern both races stand as filed: Mississippi’s affidavit identification is due November 10 and its counties certify by November 13, and the candidate with the most votes wins; Alaska takes domestic mail ballots until November 13 and overseas ballots until November 18, and its ranked-choice tabulation is scheduled for November 18.

The House count crept again in the evening, and the call desks end the day farther apart in arithmetic and in agreement on everything else. The Associated Press tracker’s latest state, as the Evening Watch printed it, shows 248 seats won by the Democrats and 13 more led, against 154 won and 20 led for the Republicans. The live results file’s check at 22:45 CET runs the called figure higher: 251 House seats called for the Democrats and 155 for the Republicans, with 29 still uncalled. Newsmax’s Thursday account runs it higher still, on a projection: the Associated Press projects the Democrats will win 252 seats, with 19 races still uncalled, 38 seats flipped, and the party’s highest House total since 2009; the Republicans, in the same account, flipped only one seat in a district unaffected by mid-decade redistricting, Maine’s 2nd. The three files were taken at different hours by different methods—seats won, seats called, seats projected—and the desk prints them as three bearings, not one number. The governorships stand at 28 for the Democrats with Alaska and Kansas open. Kansas stands where it stood: the Democrat, Cindy Holscher, ahead by 7,045 votes with all precincts reporting, the close-race audits ordered, the race uncalled.

Colorado, Corrected in the Open

Colorado’s 3rd District has changed hands since this paper last printed it whole, and the correction is the midnight file’s first duty. The Midnight Watch of November 5 and the editions that followed carried the Democrat, Dwayne Romero, leading the incumbent Republican, Jeff Hurd, by more than 2,200 votes, on the Colorado live file as it signed off on election night, when Romero did lead. The lead changed hands overnight, as the district’s remaining vote came in, and on Thursday it widened in the incumbent’s favor. The state results file, carrying the secretary of state’s figures and updated at 5:25 p.m. MST, puts Hurd at 162,669 votes, 49.31 percent, and Romero at 156,472, 47.43 percent—a margin of 6,197 votes. Decision Desk HQ’s file at 9:07 p.m. EST runs the same order slightly wider: Hurd 163,655, Romero 157,523, a margin of 6,132 in a count of 332,044 votes. The Associated Press district file carries the state’s figures and labels the race too early to call, at 96.73 percent of precincts reporting. The margin stands outside the half-percent threshold that would require a recount. The leader this paper printed on Wednesday was the leader of Wednesday’s count; the leader of Thursday’s count is Hurd, and the log records the change where it happened, in the open.

Colorado’s 4th District narrowed all day and ends it uncalled, with the incumbent’s strongest county finished counting. The state’s figures at 5:25 p.m. MST put the Democrat, Eileen Laubacher, at 184,024 votes and the incumbent Republican, Lauren Boebert, at 180,758—a margin of 3,266. Decision Desk HQ’s file at 9:56 p.m. EST puts the same pair at 184,624 and 181,555—a margin of 3,069, in a count of 378,685 votes, more than 95 percent of the expected vote. A later account of the state results, filed below, puts the lead at 2,376 votes and records the fact the remaining arithmetic turns on: Weld County, which gives Boebert her largest county lead, 20,074 votes to 13,572, has finished counting except for ballots with signature problems and ballots forwarded from other counties, and the ballots still out are concentrated in Douglas, Larimer, and Arapahoe counties, which Laubacher is carrying. The district’s own paper counts at least about 7,000 ballots remaining in the four most populous counties as of 5:30 p.m. and 474 ballots in Weld awaiting signature cures. Signature fixes and military and overseas ballots are due by 11:59 p.m. on November 12, and the counties finish tabulating on November 13. The Associated Press has not called the race.

After the Close: The Futures, Then Tokyo

The evening trade continued the day’s direction, at a slower speed, in two readings that do not match. The early-evening account, carrying CNBC’s figures, records S&P 500 futures and Nasdaq-100 futures each down 0.4 percent and Dow futures down 201 points, or 0.4 percent. The later account, in the same wire’s figures at a later hour, records S&P 500 futures down 0.8 percent, Nasdaq-100 futures down 1.3 percent, and Dow futures down 264 points, or 0.5 percent. Both accounts name the same subjects in front of the market: the October payrolls report, due Friday at 8:30 a.m. ET, and the concern, stated in the later account, that the Democratic victory could slow the pace of the data-center and artificial-intelligence buildout. No floor was reported in either account. The futures are a reading, not a close, and the desk files them as a reading.

By the hour Washington reached midnight, Tokyo was already in its Friday afternoon, and Friday there opened with the same selling, in larger size. The Nikkei 225, which had closed Thursday at 61,077.9 in the figures carried in the Tokyo–Seoul account filed below, gapped down at the open to 60,374.35 and fell 6.2 percent to 57,288.91. A second account of the Tokyo morning carries the fall deeper: an intraday low of 56,745.81, down 7 percent, and the index 5.7 percent lower at 57,579 at 11:18 a.m. in Tokyo. The index closed above 72,000 for the first time in late June; a fall of more than 20 percent from that record puts it in a bear market, and both accounts record it there. The names are the supply chain of the same buildout: Advantest down 12 percent, SoftBank Group down 11 percent, Kioxia down 11 percent, and Tokyo Electron down nearly 9 percent, in CNBC’s figures carried in the accounts. In Seoul the Kospi fell 8.55 percent to 4,923.47, below 5,000, and a Level 1 circuit breaker halted trading for twenty minutes; Samsung Electronics fell 10.07 percent to 181,200 won and SK Hynix fell 12.26 percent to 1,109,000 won. Taiwan’s Taiex fell more than 8 percent in its session before recovering part of the fall, and the Shanghai Composite stood down 1.1 percent and the Hang Seng down 0.60 percent in the Tokyo-morning snapshot. No new American fact arrived in the night to explain the Asian session. The explanation the accounts give is the one Thursday gave in New York: the election, read as a check on the buildout, priced a second time—this time on the other side of the Pacific, on the next day’s date.

Oil at Midnight: Brent Toward a Hundred Again

The settlement is fixed, and the evening trade carried Brent past it. Brent crude futures settled on Thursday up $3.67, or 3.88 percent, at $98.29 a barrel, and West Texas Intermediate closed up $2.40 at $90.52, per Reuters’ New York file as the Evening Watch printed it. In the hours after the settlement, Reuters’ early-Friday file records Brent futures for January up $1.57, or 1.6 percent, at $99.86 a barrel as of 0222 GMT, and West Texas Intermediate up $1.10 at $91.62; the Tokyo-morning account carries an evening-session high of $99.62. The same Reuters file holds the week’s other bearing in the same paragraph: Brent remains on track to fall about 12 percent for the week, after the December contract’s expiry on October 30, and the rebound of Wednesday and Thursday is recorded as a rebound on the surge in tanker attacks in the Gulf and the strait. Flows through the Strait of Hormuz, in that file’s figure, run under 60 percent of capacity.

The tanker file grew on Thursday, in claims, and the claims are filed as claims. Iran’s Revolutionary Guards, in their Operational Statement No. 21, said two tankers and a tugboat caught fire after using unauthorized routes through the strait—one tanker on a naval mine in the southern passage and a supertanker on fire in the eastern strait. Later on Thursday Iran’s regular navy reported three additional tanker incidents, vessels said to have struck naval mines in restricted waters east of the strait, per the account of the expanded claims filed below; the Iranian claims for Thursday thus stand at five tankers and a tugboat. Reuters’ Dubai file records the measured file beside them: at least five vessels have reported incidents since Sunday, according to the British maritime security agency UKMTO—about the pace of October, when the agency counted 35 vessels hit, the most of any month of the war—and a vessel was struck by two unidentified projectiles late on Wednesday, placed in the expanded account at about 50 nautical miles north of Madinat ash-Shamal in Qatar. No independent confirmation of the three additional Thursday incidents appears in any file the desk took in the evening. South Korea’s Defence Ministry said it will deploy maritime patrol aircraft and an explosive ordnance disposal team to waters near the strait, per the account of the strait’s week filed below, which records that South Korea sourced 70 percent of its oil from the Middle East in 2025 and that Iran has warned South Korea against the deployment. No agreement was announced on Thursday. The mediation stands where the midday and evening editions left it—Qatar’s efforts intensified, both governments reviewing proposals, Tehran’s conditions stated, per the mediation account—and Eurasia Group’s odds, carried at evening, stand unrevised at midnight: a deal at 10 percent, renewed American strikes at 60 percent, a continued standoff at 30 percent.

Washington at Midnight

The positions filed on Thursday stand unchanged at midnight, and the evening’s new paper is arithmetic. The president’s two halves—he will get along with the Democrats unless they want to be destructive, and he holds the power of the veto—stand as the Evening Watch printed them, with his answer on impeachment, “not even a little bit.” The incoming majority’s program stands as filed: affordability first, the Medicaid changes reversed, the lapsed health-insurance credits restored, and the funding bills used to limit the administration and the war. The evening account of what happens next, filed below, works the arithmetic both sides are working from: most legislation needs 60 votes to clear the Senate and then the president’s signature; overriding a veto takes two-thirds of both chambers, 67 votes in the Senate, which the majority does not hold; the House can impeach by a simple majority and the Senate can remove only by the same 67; and the power that changes hands whole on January 3 is the Senate’s power to confirm or refuse the president’s nominees. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand, on NPR’s Morning Edition on Thursday, stated the majority’s order in her own words, per the account of the interview filed below: lowering costs, restoring health care access, and ending the war in Iran; on the Medicaid restoration, “I dare him to veto that”; on impeachment, no commitment; and, on doing accountability and legislation together, “We can do both.”

The calendar the lame duck will run on is settled, and its first deadline is today. House Republicans’ candidates for their leadership elections must declare by today, Friday, November 6; the elections themselves are set for Tuesday, November 10, in both parties’ House conferences and in the Senate Republican conference, as the Evening Watch filed. Congress returns on Monday, November 9, for the lame-duck session. The government is funded through Friday, December 11, under the stopgap the president signed on September 2, Public Law 119-103, per the funding account filed below; twelve fiscal 2027 appropriations bills stand unfinished, the House having passed three and the Senate none in the accounting carried in the funding files, and the largest sticking point recorded is defense spending, against a request of about $1.5 trillion. Money for the war with Iran is recorded in the same files as the largest item on the outgoing majority’s wish list for the session. None of that business was transacted on Thursday. It is the work the log hands to the week that begins on Monday.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings never give a point; they give a small triangle, and this paper prints the triangle. First, the House at midnight: 248 seats won and 13 led in the Associated Press tracker’s latest state, 251 called in the live file’s evening check, and 252 projected with 19 uncalled in the Newsmax account—three methods, three hours, one chamber, and agreement on the outcome and on nothing smaller. Third, the strait: five vessels reporting incidents since Sunday in the British agency’s count, against five tankers and a tugboat claimed by Iran for Thursday alone—a count of reports and a count of claims, printed side by side because they are not the same kind of number. Fourth, Friday’s test arrives with a spread already on it: the October payrolls forecasts stand at about 55,000 in one survey, 59,000 in the Dow Jones consensus, and 65,000 in another, per the preview of the report filed below, against September’s 29,000 and an unemployment rate expected to hold at 4.2 percent—with the private ADP report, already in, at 86,000 jobs added against 75,000 expected. Against the triangle, the load-bearing facts of the day are single-valued: no Senate race was called on Thursday; the Dow closed down 1,833.06 points and the Nasdaq Composite down 5.52 percent, in correction; Brent settled at $98.29; Bank Rate stands at 4 percent; jobless claims stand at 189,000; Colorado’s 3rd District is led by its Republican incumbent; and the payrolls report is due at 8:30 a.m. The count belongs to the clerks until November 13 in Colorado and Mississippi and November 18 in Alaska. The log proceeds to Friday.

What the Log Leaves Open

The last entry of the day closes with the open file, stated plainly. The October employment report, today at 8:30 a.m. ET, with a forecast spread of 55,000 to 65,000 jobs around a consensus of 59,000. The House leadership declarations, due today. The leadership elections and Mississippi’s affidavit deadline, on November 10. Colorado’s cure and overseas-ballot deadline at 11:59 p.m. on November 12, and its counties’ final tabulation and Mississippi’s certification on November 13. Nvidia’s earnings on November 17. Alaska’s ranked-choice tabulation on November 18. The Federal Reserve’s last meeting of the year on December 9, at which traders, in the preview’s CME figures, price a 67 percent chance of a further 25-basis-point increase. The funding expiry on December 11. The Congress that convenes on January 3. Beneath the calendar, the same open questions the day began with: two Senate seats, two governorships, and between 19 and 29 House races, on the clerks’ schedules; the final size of a majority every file agrees on; and the end of the war, which no agreement announced on Thursday. Until those counts and that Congress settle them, they stand in the log as open. The day is filed. The log turns.

entry.title: The Second Reading: The Chips Fall Twelve Percent and the Buildout Is Repriced
entry.summary: A special report from the desk, filed outside the watches: on Wednesday the market bought the midterm result; on Thursday it sold the same result. The Nasdaq fell 5.52 percent into correction, the semiconductor index fell 12.25 percent, and the ballot record on data centers reached the tape.
entry.content:
Special Report

The Markets File — The Second Reading of an Election

Objective

The Second Reading: The Chips Fall Twelve Percent and the Buildout Is Repriced

On Wednesday the market read the midterm results and bought. On Thursday it read them again and sold. The two closes, the ballot record underneath them, and the governments the voters chose, in one file, outside the watches.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 1912 ET, Thursday, November 5, 2026. The day’s complete record—the count, the strait, the considered responses of every side—stands in Edition No. 8, the Evening Watch. This report stands the market story on its own.

The Two Closes

The same election was priced twice in two sessions, and the second price erased the first and went past it. On Wednesday, the first session after the midterms, the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 1,569.40 points, or 3.0 percent, to 53,356.12; the S&P 500 rose 1.6 percent to 7,688.62; the Nasdaq Composite rose 1.4 percent to 25,736.51. On Thursday the Dow fell 1,833.06 points to 51,523.06; the S&P 500 fell 4.36 percent to 7,353.73, its worst day since April 2025; the Nasdaq Composite fell 5.52 percent to 24,315.00. All three indexes closed below their levels of Tuesday, election day, and the Nasdaq’s close stands 11.9 percent below its record close of October 6—inside correction territory, by the usual definition.

IndexWednesday, Nov. 4Thursday, Nov. 5
Dow Jones Industrial Average+1,569.40 (+3.0%) · 53,356.12−1,833.06 (−3.44%) · 51,523.06
S&P 500+1.6% · 7,688.62−4.36% · 7,353.73
Nasdaq Composite+1.4% · 25,736.51−5.52% · 24,315.00

No result changed between the two sessions. The ballots counted on Wednesday morning were the ballots counted on Thursday morning. What changed was the reading. Wednesday’s session priced the election as an event completed. Thursday’s session priced it as a program begun: a Congress of the other party, governors elected on stated intentions toward the data-center buildout, and a ballot record, assembled measure by measure across ten states, in which voters had answered the buildout directly. The desk states the sequence because the sequence is the fact: the votes were counted first, the governments changed second, and the capital was repriced third.

What Fell on Thursday

The selling was led by the companies that build the artificial-intelligence infrastructure, and it was the largest single-day destruction of market value on record. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 12.25 percent to 9,011.14, its second-worst fall on record. SanDisk fell 22 percent; Advanced Micro Devices fell 17.26 percent; Micron and Marvell fell about 17 percent each; Broadcom fell 10.43 percent; Nvidia fell 9.26 percent to $181.60, erasing its gains for the year; Qualcomm fell 9.5 percent. Roughly $2.5 trillion of value left the Nasdaq Composite and roughly $2.9 trillion left the companies of the S&P 500, each a single-day record in the accounts filed; the seven largest technology companies lost about $1.04 trillion among them. The volatility index rose 69 percent to 28.18.

The falls were lopsided, and the lopsidedness is part of the record. The companies that own computing capacity fell far less than the companies that build it or finance it. Meta Platforms fell 3.4 percent. The neocloud companies, which borrow to build capacity and rent it out—CoreWeave and Nebius—fell between 10 and 17.6 percent; the data-center operators IREN, Hut 8, and Applied Digital fell between 6 and 11 percent; Tesla fell 11 percent. The market did not sell the use of the machines at the rate it sold the making of them.

The Ballot Record

On Tuesday, in ten states, the buildout itself was on the ballot, and the answers were recorded precinct by precinct. Forty-one local measures on data-center construction were put to voters in California, Florida, Illinois, Kansas, Maine, Nevada, New Jersey, North Dakota, Ohio, and Wisconsin. In the fullest tracker the desk can file—Ballotpedia’s, with results for all forty-one—forty went the way of tighter limits: bans adopted, moratoriums approved, rezoning refused, measures that would have eased construction rejected. The one exception was Harwood, North Dakota, where voters rejected an added review requirement for large industrial projects by 325 votes to 105. Some of the measures are binding law and some are advisory; the desk prints them as one record because the voters cast them as one.

The margins were not narrow. Kansas wrote its definitions into the questions—a high-impact facility is one drawing more than 10 megawatts of peak electricity or more than 100,000 gallons of water a day—and El Dorado adopted a ten-year ban by 71 to 29, Emporia a prohibition by 60 to 40, and Ottawa a ban on facilities above 25 megawatts by 69 to 31. In Alhambra, California, 82 percent voted to ban data centers from the city. In Joliet, Illinois, 79 percent answered no to an advisory question asking the city to approve them, and 88 percent of Morgan County, Illinois, backed restrictions. Ohio carried twenty-one of the forty-one measures, the most of any state: in Wilmington, rezoning for a data-center project was rejected by roughly four votes to one, and in Hubbard more than three-quarters approved a ban. Edgewater, Florida, voted that no new data centers be built there. An Ohio effort to place a constitutional amendment banning new construction on next year’s statewide ballot is under way. The record is not closed: Clarksville, Arkansas, decides data-center bond questions on December 1, and Mandan, North Dakota, votes on a ban covering facilities of 25 megawatts or more on December 15.

The Governments the Voters Chose

The partisan result is stated as the counts stand on Thursday evening. The Democrats will organize both chambers of the Congress that convenes on January 3. The Senate stands at 54 seats for the Democrats and 44 for the Republicans, with Alaska and Mississippi uncalled and the Democratic candidate leading in each. The Associated Press House tracker in its latest state shows 248 seats won by the Democrats and 13 more led, against 154 won and 20 led for the Republicans. The governorships stand at 28 for the Democrats, with Alaska and Kansas open, and by Ballotpedia’s accounting the party will hold 21 state trifectas—the most it has held since 1992.

In the state where the buildout is concentrated, the governorship changed hands on the question. Texas holds the largest share of planned American data-center capacity. Its voters elected the Democrat, Gina Hinojosa, over the incumbent Republican governor, Greg Abbott, after she promised a moratorium on new data-center construction. In Georgia, Keisha Lance Bottoms won the governorship after calling for a pause on new data centers. In Ohio, the state with twenty-one measures on its local ballots, the Democrat, Amy Acton, won the governorship. What the incoming Congress will do with the buildout has not been filed as legislation; what is on the record is the expectation, stated by the analysts quoted in the clippings below, of scrutiny of the construction program, and a bank’s estimate, carried in the morning file, that about 30 percent of the data-center additions expected in 2028 stand at risk from pauses.

What Did Not Happen, and What Comes Next

No collapse in demand for the technology was reported on Thursday, and no company at the center of the fall reported one. AMD fell 17.26 percent two days after guiding its results above expectations. Qualcomm’s Wednesday disappointment, the one company-specific result in the chain, was in smartphone chips and the rising cost of memory, a different ledger from the data centers. The day’s economic figures ran the other way: initial claims for unemployment benefits stood at 189,000, the lowest reading since 1969, as the Evening Watch filed. The reported trigger of the repricing was not an earnings statement. It was the election, read the second time.

The calendar ahead is fixed, and the desk prints it as the file’s last entry. Friday at 8:30 a.m. ET brings the October employment report. On November 10 the House parties hold their leadership elections and Mississippi’s affidavit identification falls due; Mississippi certifies on November 13. Nvidia reports on November 17. Alaska’s ranked-choice tabulation is scheduled for November 18. The Arkansas and North Dakota data-center votes follow on December 1 and December 15. The Congress whose scrutiny the market priced on Thursday convenes on January 3.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings never give a point; they give a small triangle, and this paper prints the triangle. The ballot record carries one. A Wednesday-morning tally counted thirty-eight of the forty-one measures decided, thirty-seven of them for limits. Ballotpedia’s tracker, complete at forty-one, counts forty for limits. A New York Post accounting counted at least fifty measures, forty-seven decided against the buildout. The tallies were taken at different hours, over different definitions of what counts as a data-center measure; they do not agree on the size of the record, and they agree on its direction—no tally on the shelf runs the other way. Against the triangle, the single-valued facts of this report are the two closes: on Wednesday the Dow rose 1,569.40 points; on Thursday it fell 1,833.06. The results did not change. The reading did. The log proceeds to the Midnight Watch.

The Clippings Filed With This Report

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this report stamped objective. Six items.

Subjective
Reuters — the tech rout and the retreat from the AI trade

The wire’s market commentary on the rout: the semiconductor index down as much as 11 percent in the session, Qualcomm’s miss at the head of the chain, and a senior analyst at Swissquote Bank stating the political reading—that the two years of federal push behind the AI buildout may now be scaled back, with scrutiny of the construction program expected.

Subjective
CNN — the sell-off and the $2.5 trillion

The account of the day’s losses: roughly $2.5 trillion of value wiped from the Nasdaq Composite, the index closing in correction at 5.52 percent down, the chip index down 12.3 percent, and the Texas governorship named as central to the selling because of the data-center construction concentrated in that state.

Subjective
MarketSpeaker — the closing account

The closing figures in one file: the Nasdaq 100 down 6.36 percent, the S&P 500 down 4.36 percent, the Dow down 1,833.06 points, the volatility gauge surged, and Wednesday’s post-election gains more than erased.

Subjective
Route Fifty — voters reject data centers in local initiatives

The election-night account of the local votes: more than forty measures across ten states, the opponents of data-center development successful in virtually all of them, Ohio carrying the most initiatives, some votes advisory rather than binding, and Harwood, North Dakota, the single place the facilities prevailed.

Subjective
Reason — the measures, state by state

The breakdown of the forty-one measures by state—twenty-one in Ohio, seven in Illinois, four in Maine, three in Kansas, and one each in six further states—with the local outcomes named: the bans in Alhambra and Edgewater, the moratorium advised in Bloomington, and the two Ohio exceptions argued the other way.

Subjective
Ballotpedia’s tracker, in a running account

The running account of the tracker’s results: all forty-one measures decided, forty of them for tighter limits, forty-six of forty-seven across the whole of 2026; the widest and closest margins named; the Texas and Georgia governorships carried with them; and the three votes still to come, in Arkansas on December 1 and North Dakota on December 15.

entry.title: The Rally Erased: The Chips Fall, Oil Rises on Tankers, the Count Creeps On
entry.summary: The evening file for November 5, 2026: the Dow falls 1,833 points and erases Wednesday's rally, the Nasdaq enters correction, Brent settles at $98.29 after tanker reports in the Strait of Hormuz, no Senate race is called, and the leadership contests are set. Edition No. 8, the Evening Watch.
entry.content:
The Midterm Elections — The Evening File

Objective

The Rally Erased: The Chips Fall, Oil Rises on Tankers, the Count Creeps On

The day’s developments whole at 1800: Wall Street gives back all of Wednesday’s post-election rally and more, the semiconductor index falls twelve percent, Brent settles up $3.67 after reports of tankers hit in the Strait of Hormuz, no Senate race is called for a second full day, the House count creeps upward in the afternoon, and every side files its considered response—the president with his veto, the incoming majority with its program, Tehran with its answer to the vice president.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 1800 ET, Thursday, November 5, 2026. This edition completes the day continued in Edition No. 6, the Overnight Watch and Edition No. 7, the Midday Watch. Those editions stand unrevised, as a log stands. Where the evening figures differ from the noon figures, the difference is stated here, in the open.

The Count at Evening

No Senate race was called on Thursday, for the second full day. The Associated Press Senate file in its latest state still lists Alaska and Mississippi as too early to call, and the chamber stands where it stood on Wednesday: 54 seats for the Democrats and 44 for the Republicans. The margins underneath the two open races did not move in any file the desk could take in the afternoon. Mississippi’s Democrat, Scott Colom, leads the incumbent Republican, Cindy Hyde-Smith, by between 1,138 and 1,852 votes depending on the tally and its hour, as the midday edition printed; affidavit identification is due by November 10 and counties certify by November 13, and the candidate with the most votes wins—there is no runoff in this race. Alaska’s Democrat, Mary Peltola, leads the incumbent Republican, Dan Sullivan, by 637 first-choice votes, with a second candidate named Daniel Sullivan holding more votes than the margin; the ranked-choice tabulation is scheduled for November 18. Control of neither chamber is in question in any count on the shelf.

The House count crept upward in the afternoon, and the call desks still do not agree on how much of it has been called. The Associated Press House tracker in its latest state shows 248 seats won by the Democrats and 13 more led, against 154 won and 20 led for the Republicans. A live results file updated at 2:44 p.m. EST runs the called figure higher: 252 seats for the Democrats and 160 for the Republicans, 412 of 435 races called, with 23 still counting. The Independent’s live file recorded House races projected for the Democrats during the day—Luz Rivas in California, Sam Forstag in Montana, and Shannon Taylor in Virginia among them—and carried a projected total of 247 Democrats to 147 Republicans at its hour. The three files were taken at different hours from different call desks. They disagree about the called total by as much as ten seats. They agree that the Democrats will organize the House in January, and that the final majority will not be known until the western counts finish.

Colorado supplied the afternoon’s one new House call and the evening’s closest watched count. The Associated Press called Colorado’s 5th District for the Democrat, Jessica Killin, on Thursday afternoon—the first Democrat to win the district since it was created in 1972—per the state results file carrying the secretary of state’s figures, updated at 1:11 p.m. MST. In the 4th District the same file, on the state’s figures, puts the Democrat, Eileen Laubacher, at 176,427 votes and the incumbent Republican, Lauren Boebert, at 174,173—a margin of 2,254 votes, narrower than the 2,513 the wire and Decision Desk HQ carried at midday—with twenty of the district’s twenty-one counties still counting and the race still too early to call. Kansas’s governorship stands where the midday edition left it: the Democrat, Cindy Holscher, ahead by 7,045 votes with all precincts reporting, the close-race audits ordered, the race uncalled. The governorships stand at 28 for the Democrats with Alaska and Kansas open.

The Markets at the Close

Thursday’s session erased Wednesday’s rally and went past it. The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed down 1,833.06 points, or 3.44 percent, at 51,523.06—against a gain of 1,569.40 points the day before. The S&P 500 closed down 4.36 percent at 7,353.73, its worst day since April 2025. The Nasdaq Composite closed down 5.52 percent at 24,315.00, in correction territory, 11.9 percent below its October 6 record close. The Nasdaq 100 closed down 6.36 percent at 26,629.81. The figures agree across the closing account filed below and the wire’s reporting through the day. The volatility index, the market’s fear gauge, closed at 28.09, up 69.1 percent from Wednesday’s 16.61. Treasury prices rose as shares fell; the ten-year yield slipped about six basis points to roughly 4.84 percent. The midday edition recorded the turn beginning—the Dow up 0.62 percent at the opening bell and down 1.67 percent at 10:41 a.m.—and the close completed it.

The selling began in the chips and did not stop there. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 12.25 percent to 9,011.14, per the closing account carrying Bloomberg’s figures; Reuters’ market commentary records the index down as much as 11 percent in the session, its worst performance since March 2020. Reuters’ news file names the trigger and the chain: Qualcomm fell 9 percent after its fourth-quarter smartphone chip sales came in below estimates; the data-center operators IREN, Hut 8, and Applied Digital fell between 6 and 11 percent; the neocloud companies CoreWeave and Nebius shed 9.3 and 13.4 percent; the server maker Dell fell 10.5 percent; Tesla fell 9.5 percent. The closing account adds the largest falls: SanDisk down 22.3 percent, Advanced Micro Devices down 17.3 percent, Nvidia down 9.3 percent. A senior analyst at Swissquote Bank, quoted in the wire’s file, stated the political reading in plain terms: “There is now a chance that the two years of extra push from the Trump government for AI buildout will somehow be scaled back… We suspect there is going to be some scrutiny on this aggressive AI buildout.” The ballot record underneath that reading is the one this paper filed on Wednesday: 41 local measures on data-center construction across ten states, with the restricting measures passing or leading in the counts so far. A UBS note carried in the morning put about 30 percent of expected 2028 data-center additions at risk from pauses in the buildout.

The day’s economic figures ran the other way, and the desk prints them beside the close because both are the day. Reuters’ report of the Labor Department’s morning releases records initial claims for unemployment benefits down 6,000 to 189,000 for the week ended October 31—the lowest reading since 1969, matched only in mid-July—against a forecast of 196,000, and third-quarter nonfarm productivity up at a 3.6 percent annualized rate against a forecast of 2.8 percent, with unit labor costs down 0.7 percent. The same report states the limit on the good news: hiring remains constrained, and the claims report has no bearing on Friday’s October employment report, which is due at 8:30 a.m. ET and is the next test the market has set itself. From the Federal Reserve, Cleveland President Beth Hammack stated on Thursday that she favored a gradual rate-hike path to lower inflation, per the wire’s file; Richmond President Thomas Barkin, in remarks carried in the day’s market digest, called inflation the most important risk for the Fed right now, said the AI buildout has had an inflationary impact in the near term, called credit dynamics in the banking sector reassuring at this point, and said he had no point of view about what will happen to fiscal policy following the election. Traders currently expect the Fed to raise rates next month, following the September increase. In London, the Bank of England’s morning decision stands as the midday edition filed it: Bank Rate raised to 4 percent from 3.75 percent by 8–1, the dissent voting for 4.25 percent, with at least one more increase likely if the conflict between the United States and Iran continues.

Oil and the Strait

Oil reversed Wednesday’s fall at the settlement, on reports of tankers hit in the Strait of Hormuz. Reuters’ New York file records Brent crude futures settled up $3.67, or 3.88 percent, at $98.29 a barrel, and West Texas Intermediate closed up $2.40, or 2.72 percent, at $90.52—the first rise in four sessions, after both benchmarks fell more than 8 percent on Wednesday to their lowest settlements since August 31. The morning’s figures, printed in the midday edition, had Brent between $93.65 and $97 depending on the hour and the feed; the settlement is the day’s fixed point. The analysts quoted give the reason as caution: a note from Gelber and Associates, carried in the file, states that the rebound reflects caution about pricing in a rapid normalization of oil flows before diplomatic progress becomes dependable shipping. Eurasia Group’s revised odds, carried in the same file, cut the probability of a deal to 10 percent from 20 percent, cut the chance of renewed American strikes to 60 percent from 65 percent, raised a continued standoff to 30 percent from 15 percent, and stated that escalation could push Brent into a $110 to $125 range.

The tanker reports are claims, and the desk files them as claims, from each side that made them. Reuters’ Gulf file records that at least five vessels have reported incidents since Sunday, according to the British maritime security agency UKMTO—about the pace of October, when the agency counted 35 vessels hit, the most of any month of the war—and that a vessel was struck by two unidentified projectiles late on Wednesday. Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said two tankers had struck naval mines and another had caught fire on Thursday; in the oil file’s version, the Guards said two oil tankers and a tugboat caught fire in separate incidents after attempting to use unauthorized routes through the strait. The two versions do not match in detail, and no independent confirmation of the Thursday incidents appears in either file. Saudi Arabia issued alerts on Thursday warning of potential danger in Yanbu, its Red Sea export hub, as Yemen’s Houthis continued attacks on the kingdom; the Houthis later said they attacked King Fahd airport in Dammam, and there was no immediate confirmation from the Saudi authorities. Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, discussed the latest progress in diplomatic efforts in separate calls with his Saudi and Qatari counterparts, per the foreign ministry statement carried in the oil file.

No agreement was announced on Thursday, and the state of the talks at evening is the state the midday edition left, with Tehran’s answer to the vice president added. The mediation account filed with the midday edition stands: Qatar has intensified its efforts, both governments are reviewing the mediators’ proposals, Tehran’s conditions—removal of oil sanctions, an end to the American naval blockade, and the release of frozen assets—must be met before the strait reopens, and a senior Iranian official’s statement that the two sides remain a considerable distance from a deal has not been withdrawn. The new entry is political. Iran’s parliament speaker, Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf, answered Vice President Vance’s post of Wednesday—the post that named the war as the reason for the Republican defeat—in the Gulf file’s account: he accused the vice president of letting the president double down like a “losing gambler” by planning more strikes, and said, “Skip the TED talk. Why not say this to your boss?” Two sources told Reuters they believed the president was still likely to order resumed hostilities, one of them stating: “He is planning to bomb Iran. Don’t listen to what he’s saying. He held off because of the midterms.” The sources are unnamed and the statement is theirs. Iran’s supreme leader, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, said on Wednesday that there should not be “even the slightest inclination towards submission” to the United States, which he said would remain hostile towards Iran no matter which party was in power. The strait, the blockade, the sanctions, and the nuclear program remain the four subjects of the mediation, in that file’s summary, and none of the four moved on Thursday.

Washington at Evening: The Considered Responses

The president’s considered position at evening has two halves, and both are on the record in his own words. Reuters’ Washington file carries the morning-after appearance at the White House ballroom site: “I’ll get along probably with the Democrats, unless they want to be destructive, but I have the power of the veto.” The account of his further remarks filed below adds the sharper versions: to Fox News, “They’re really not in control because they can send over, you know, 50 different great bills that they’re all excited about, and I send them back with a nice stamp veto”; to Politico, “I don’t want to be just sitting there for two years vetoing everything”; and, asked whether he was concerned about a third impeachment attempt, “not even a little bit,” with the warning that it would “destroy” the Democratic Party if they tried. He said he will work with the Democrats to make sure things go well for the country. The two halves do not cancel each other. They are the negotiating position of a president who has lost both chambers and kept the veto, stated by the president himself on the second day.

The incoming majority’s considered response describes the same bargain from the other side. The account of the Democratic leaders’ planning filed below records House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries at an afternoon press conference on Wednesday: Democrats “are ready, willing and able to find bipartisan common ground with the other side of the aisle as long as we can bring about meaningful change on the issues that matter. And that begins with decisively addressing the affordability crisis.” The same account records the to-do list the majority says it will begin with—reversing the Medicaid changes in the president’s tax-and-spending law and restoring the enhanced Affordable Care Act tax credits that lapsed at the end of last year—and Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer’s stated priorities: lowering the cost of living, cleaning up corruption in government, acting as a check on the administration, and using the annual government funding bills to impose limits on the administration and on the war in Iran. On impeachment, Jeffries repeated the sentence he has given every questioner: “I haven’t had a single member of the House Democratic Caucus talk to me about impeachment. We’ve been relentlessly focused on affordability and on accountability.” The account states the arithmetic both sides are working from: the majority will not hold veto-proof margins, so any major legislation will need the president’s signature. The program and the veto are now both on paper. What they produce together is the work of the Congress that convenes on January 3.

The Republican Party’s internal business for the week is a leadership election, and its date is set. The Daily Caller’s account records that Speaker Mike Johnson announced on Wednesday that he will not seek a leadership role in the next Congress, and that Majority Leader Steve Scalise and Judiciary Committee chairman Jim Jordan launched bids the same day to become the party’s next leader. House Republicans hold their leadership elections on Tuesday, November 10, with candidates required to declare by November 6; Majority Whip Tom Emmer has told colleagues he will run for whip in the minority, and Republican Study Committee chairman August Pfluger is challenging him for that post, per the accounts filed below. Scalise’s letter to the conference, quoted in the Caller, states his case in one sentence: “I am ready to lead on day one and chart our path back to the majority.” In the Senate, Republicans hold their leadership elections on November 10 as well, and Majority Leader John Thune is expected to run again, per the accounts. Jeffries made his own bid for the speakership official in a Dear Colleague letter on Wednesday. The gavels change hands in January; the contests for who will hold the minority’s are decided next week.

The World at Evening

The foreign responses filed by evening sort into the same three groups as Wednesday’s, with the positions now stated by governments rather than parties. Al Jazeera’s roundup of the world’s reactions leads with Tehran: parliament speaker Ghalibaf’s post—“Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message”—and the supreme leader’s statement that partisan shifts in Washington will not alter American hostility towards Iran. In Europe, European Parliament vice president Christel Schaldemose said the results left her “cautiously optimistic on Europe’s behalf”; Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, called the Democratic victory emblematic of the unravelling of the global far right; Britain’s prime minister, Andy Burnham, said the results presented an opportunity for world leaders to work together to ease cost-of-living pressures and resolve the conflict in the Middle East, per the account of the foreign leaders’ responses filed below; France’s finance minister, Roland Lescure, said Paris would wait to see whether the president, who remains in control of American foreign policy, adjusts his approach. Russia’s deputy foreign minister, Sergey Ryabkov, noted that the Democratic Party’s leaders had a sharply negative approach to relations with Moscow, and Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Moscow hoped the results would not impact the president’s peacemaking efforts. South Africa’s president, Cyril Ramaphosa, said the election marks a new era in world relations. Japan’s chief cabinet secretary, Minoru Kihara, emphasized that the Japan–United States alliance stands. In Israel, where the prime minister’s coalition lost its own parliamentary majority last week, there was no immediate reaction from Benjamin Netanyahu; Yair Golan, of a coalition seeking to replace him, said the American vote reveals how toxic Netanyahu has become among American Democrats and Republicans alike. Every capital read the same election. Each read it as a sentence about itself, and the desk files the readings as readings.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings never give a point; they give a small triangle, and this paper prints the triangle. First, the House: 248 seats won and 13 led in the Associated Press tracker’s latest state, 252 called for the Democrats in a live file updated at 2:44 p.m., and 247 projected in the Independent’s file at its hour—three call desks, three hours, one chamber, and agreement only on the outcome. Second, Colorado’s 4th: a margin of 2,513 votes in the wire and Decision Desk figures carried at midday, and 2,254 in the state’s figures in the afternoon file—the leader the same, the margin narrowing as the count proceeds, the race uncalled in both. Third, the strait: five vessels reporting incidents since Sunday in the British agency’s count, two tankers on mines and a third on fire in the Revolutionary Guards’ Thursday statement, and two tankers and a tugboat on fire in the same statement as carried in a second file—the incidents claimed, the details unmatched, the confirmation absent. Against the triangle, the load-bearing facts of the evening are single-valued: no Senate race was called on Thursday; the Dow closed down 1,833 points and the Nasdaq Composite down 5.52 percent, in correction; the semiconductor index fell about twelve percent; Brent settled at $98.29, up $3.67; initial jobless claims stand at 189,000, the lowest since 1969; the Bank of England’s rate stands at 4 percent; the House Republican leadership election is set for November 10; and Friday’s employment report is due at 8:30 a.m. The count belongs to the clerks until November 10 in Mississippi and November 18 in Alaska. The log proceeds to midnight.

The Clippings Filed With This Edition

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. Twenty-three items.

Subjective
Associated Press — Senate, every state

The Senate file in its latest state: 35 races listed, Alaska and Mississippi both too early to call, and the remaining races called state by state.

Subjective
Associated Press — House balance of power

248 House seats won by Democrats and 13 more led, against 154 won and 20 led for Republicans, in the tracker’s latest state.

Subjective
Poliwave — the House live results file

Updated November 5 at 2:44 p.m. EST: 252 House seats called for Democrats and 160 for Republicans, 412 of 435 races called, with Colorado’s 4th still counting at 176,162 to 173,649.

Subjective
The Independent — the live file, Thursday

House races projected for the Democrats during the day, including Luz Rivas in California, Sam Forstag in Montana, and Shannon Taylor in Virginia, with a projected total of 247 Democrats to 147 Republicans at its hour, and the Senate at 54 to 44.

Subjective
Rocky Mountain Voice — Colorado, every race

The secretary of state’s figures, updated 1:11 p.m. MST: the 5th District called for Jessica Killin, the first Democrat to win it since 1972; the 4th District at Laubacher 176,427, Boebert 174,173, with twenty of twenty-one counties still counting.

Subjective
The Business Standard — why Alaska and Mississippi have not been called

Mississippi’s 1,138-vote margin, its November 10 and November 13 dates, no runoff in the procedure, and no automatic recount; Alaska’s mail windows and its November 18 ranked-choice tabulation.

Subjective
MarketSpeaker — the close, November 5

The closing levels: the Nasdaq 100 down 6.36 percent to 26,629.81, the Nasdaq Composite down 5.52 percent to 24,315.00, the S&P 500 down 4.36 percent to 7,353.73, and the Dow down 1,833.06 points to 51,523.06; the VIX at 28.09, up 69.1 percent; Nvidia down 9.3 percent, AMD down 17.3 percent, SanDisk down 22.3 percent; the ten-year yield down about six basis points to roughly 4.84 percent.

Subjective
Reuters, via Kitco — Wall Street slumps on chip losses

Qualcomm down 9 percent on the smartphone chip miss; the semiconductor index down 7.1 percent at its hour; IREN, Hut 8, and Applied Digital down between 6 and 11 percent; CoreWeave down 9.3 percent and Nebius down 13.4 percent; Dell down 10.5 percent; Tesla down 9.5 percent; the Swissquote analyst’s statement on scrutiny of the AI buildout; and Cleveland Fed President Hammack’s preference for a gradual rate-hike path.

Subjective
Reuters — the tech-stock rout, a market view

The semiconductor index down as much as 11 percent, its worst performance since March 2020, and the Nasdaq down as much as 5 percent; more than a dozen large technology stocks down by double digits; the ballot initiatives limiting data-center building named among the causes; the semiconductor index about 31 percent below its 52-week high, in a commentator’s figure.

Subjective
The Private Banker — the S&P 500’s worst day since April 2025

The S&P 500 down about 4.3 percent, its steepest one-day decline since April 2025; the Nasdaq Composite down 5.5 percent into correction territory, more than 10 percent below its October 6 record; the Dow down 1,833.06 points; and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index down 12.25 percent to 9,011.14.

Subjective
Reuters, via 941 The Duke — jobless claims at 57-year lows

Initial claims down 6,000 to 189,000 for the week ended October 31, against a forecast of 196,000, matching the lowest reading since 1969; continuing claims at 1.718 million; third-quarter productivity up at a 3.6 percent annualized rate against a forecast of 2.8 percent; and the statement that the claims report has no bearing on Friday’s October employment report.

Subjective
SquawkNews — the November 5 market LiveCast brief

The day’s running digest: the S&P 500 down 4.36 percent and the Nasdaq 100 down 6.36 percent; Richmond Fed President Barkin’s statements that inflation is the most important risk for the Fed right now, that the AI buildout has had an inflationary impact in the near term, that credit dynamics in the banking sector are reassuring at this point, and that he has no point of view on fiscal policy following the election.

Subjective
Reuters — the Bank of England raises rates

Bank Rate raised to 4 percent from 3.75 percent by 8–1, Catherine Mann voting for 4.25 percent; inflation expected to reach about 5 percent in the middle of next year and to return to target in the third quarter of 2028; Governor Bailey’s statement that the increase is unlikely to be the last unless the Middle East conflict is resolved.

Subjective
Reuters, via LSE — Brent settles up over $3 after tanker attacks

New York, November 5: Brent settled up $3.67, or 3.88 percent, at $98.29 a barrel, and West Texas Intermediate closed up $2.40, or 2.72 percent, at $90.52, after both fell more than 8 percent on Wednesday; five vessels reporting incidents since Sunday in the UKMTO count; Eurasia Group’s revised odds—a deal at 10 percent, renewed strikes at 60 percent, a standoff at 30 percent; the Saudi alerts at Yanbu and the Houthi claim at Dammam; and Foreign Minister Araghchi’s calls with his Saudi and Qatari counterparts.

Subjective
Reuters, via The Business Standard — tankers hit in Hormuz

Iran reports three more tankers damaged in the strait on Thursday; the UKMTO count of at least five vessels reporting incidents since Sunday; Parliament Speaker Qalibaf’s answer to the vice president—“Skip the TED talk. Why not say this to your boss?”; the supreme leader’s statement against submission; the two unnamed sources on resumed strikes; and Qatar’s statement that the United States and Iran are reviewing proposals.

Subjective
AnewZ — tensions persist as Qatar pushes for a deal

Qatar’s mediation intensified; both governments reviewing the mediators’ proposals; the senior Iranian official’s statement that the sides remain far apart and that Tehran’s conditions must precede the strait’s reopening; the 36-hour expectation for responses, and the later statement that no fixed deadline exists.

Subjective
Reuters, via The Business Standard — Democrats vow to rein in the president

The incoming majority’s focus on affordability and accountability in Jeffries’s words; the president’s ballroom appearance and his veto sentence; the war acknowledged and stood by; the vice president’s post quoted; Governor DeSantis’s extinction-level description; Speaker Johnson’s decision not to lead his caucus next year; and the lame-duck funding measure ahead.

Subjective
LADbible — the president’s warning on impeachment

The president’s statements as reported: a third impeachment attempt would destroy the Democratic Party; he is not concerned, “not even a little bit”; the Democrats are not in control because he sends their bills back with a nice stamp veto; he does not want to spend two years vetoing everything; and he will work with the Democrats to make sure things go well for the country.

Subjective
RVA Magazine, carrying States Newsroom — how the majority deals with the president

Jeffries’s afternoon statement that Democrats are ready, willing, and able to find bipartisan common ground beginning with the affordability crisis; the Medicaid reversal and the Affordable Care Act credits at the head of the to-do list; Schumer’s priorities of living costs, corruption, and a check on the administration, with funding bills used to limit the war; Jeffries’s impeachment sentence repeated; and the statement that the majority will not hold veto-proof margins.

Subjective
Daily Caller — Scalise and Jordan for the top House Republican post

Speaker Johnson’s announcement that he will not seek a leadership role; Majority Leader Scalise’s and Chairman Jordan’s bids launched Wednesday; the face-off set for Tuesday’s leadership elections; and Scalise’s sentence that he is ready to lead on day one and chart the path back to the majority.

Subjective
Reuters — futures steady, Nasdaq lags

At 5:04 a.m. ET: Dow contracts up 0.48 percent, S&P 500 contracts up 0.01 percent, Nasdaq 100 contracts down 0.63 percent; Qualcomm down 10.1 percent premarket; the UBS note putting about 30 percent of expected 2028 data-center additions at risk; three Fed officials to speak, and Friday’s October jobs report ahead.

Subjective
Al Jazeera, via EuropeSays — “Seismic shift”: the world reacts

The world’s reactions as the scale of the victory emerged: Ghalibaf’s “NO TO WAR” post and the supreme leader’s answer; Schaldemose cautiously optimistic; Sánchez on the unravelling of the global far right; Britain’s health minister on steady ties through a seismic shift; France’s finance minister waiting on the president; Ryabkov on the Democrats and Moscow; Peskov’s hope for the peacemaking efforts; Ramaphosa’s new era; and Golan on Netanyahu.

Subjective
Fox News — the foreign leaders’ claims

The responses of foreign leaders who have clashed with the president: Sánchez’s post on the rejection of the president’s agenda; Schaldemose’s cautious optimism; Burnham on cost-of-living pressures and the Middle East conflict; Japan’s chief cabinet secretary on the alliance; Ramaphosa’s new era in world relations; and the president’s congratulations and veto warning printed with them.
